newsitem.title: UK: Coffee traders plan complaint against grade change.
newsitem.headline: Coffee traders plan complaint against grade change.

text.p: Coffee traders are planning to file a complaint to the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) against changes in grading methods which they say caused them heavy losses.
On Wednesday the exchange sent a circular to members detailing how planned new specifications would come into force from July 1997.
It said the current grading specifications would be valid for deliveries until May 1997 but all previously graded coffee would have to be re-graded for deliveries from July onwards.
Traders were taken by surprise at what they said were snap changes that were announced without any prior consultation. Some are even considering asking the Exchange for compensation.
"People are planning to write a joint letter of complaint to LIFFE," said one trader.
"It's not very well handled," said another. "Nobody had been consulted or told about this before."

The changes mean traders holding graded coffee with the intention to deliver after July will have to incur an extra $20 per five-tonne lot for re-grading. Redeliveries are a common practice in the trade.
But bigger losses arose on Wednesday when the premium on the May contract against July shrank to zero from $15 on the news.

Many traders dabbling on switches rather than outright positions to minimise their risks were caught long of the May contract. For 1,000 lots of the May/July switch, for example, this meant a loss of $15,000.
"Nobody wants May coffee any more," said one. On Thursday, May was trading at $13 discount to July.
Some traders were questioning the legality of such a market-moving action by LIFFE without the consent of its members.
But LIFFE officials said Wednesday's move intended to do just that. The Exchange was giving seven months notice to members before the changes are implemented.

"The notice was put out prior to the merger (between LIFFE and the London Commodity Exchange). All we have done yesterday was to clarify the transitional arrangements," said Chris Royal, director of market operations and supervision.
He said LIFFE had taken legal advice before making the announcement, and that the changes were irreversible.

But traders said the confusion and the resulting trade speculation could have been avoided if all the implications of the grading changes in the transitional period had been clearer when the decision was first announced in March.
Many had assumed that they would be able to carry grading certificates forward. These are usually valid for three years.
The changes relate to the bands of defects for the tenderable grades and the discount awarded in the case of each band. In addition, mouldy beans were added to the list of defects.
The defect band for a Type I basis coffee has been narrowed to 0-150 defects per 500 gm from 0-225 defects per 500 gm.
